A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FastVMT, with matching core equations, experiments and figures. All supplied pages are readable. v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–G. Unresolved references in v2 are documentation defects rather than extraction gaps.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original video-generation comparisons, runtime measurements and component ablations, including quantitative results in Tables 1 and 2.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds numerical user-study results, sensitivity results and qualitative cases in its appendix.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2–3.4 retain the same motion extraction, guidance losses and gradient reuse procedure. However, new Appendix B.4 specifies an unsquared L2 window loss, conflicting with the squared loss in retained Equation 7. The PDFs do not establish whether this reflects an actual objective change or a documentation error.

E1.justification: The DAVIS evaluation and collection of 40 real and 40 generated reference videos remain unchanged. Additional illustrations largely extend existing motion categories. Appendix D.3 claims an MTBench experiment but provides only an unresolved 'Table ??' reference, without results or sufficient dataset details to establish distinct evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator set remains MOFT, MotionClone, SMM, DiTFlow, MotionInversion, MotionDirector and DeT. The appendix user-study table and additional visual comparisons use these same methods; changed citation formatting does not establish different comparators.

E3.justification: Appendix Table 3 introduces evaluation conditions varying temporal span across 3, 5 and 7. Existing main-experiment settings, metrics, video counts and the 20-participant study remain unchanged. Newly supplied default hyperparameters and questionnaire details document existing experiments rather than establish revised protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds temporal-span sensitivity results and explicit occlusion failure cases, and quantifies the existing comparison of the 10th, 15th and 20th attention layers. These extend the retained component and step-skipping analyses. Appendix Table 4 principally tabulates the VBench ablation analysis already displayed as a radar chart.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, actual seed values, confidence intervals or significance tests. Both promise future seed disclosure. The newly tabulated average user rankings provide concrete results without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The main comparison and component-ablation values are unchanged after matching the renumbered tables. The appendix substantially expands reported outcomes with user-study rankings, layer and temporal-span scores, exact VBench ablation values and qualitative cases. Newly reported overall user ranks are 2.225 for FastVMT and 3.783 for DeT; span 3 has slightly higher motion smoothness than span 5, 0.9899 versus 0.9891.

T1.justification: The main equations and complexity argument are retained. Appendix B.4 adds a non-equivalent mathematical specification using unsquared L2 temporal differences, whereas Equation 7 in both versions uses squared L2 differences. This introduces a limited formal inconsistency; no new theorem, proof or guarantee is supplied.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: removing motion and gradient redundancy through local attention windows, corresponding-window guidance and gradient reuse. The 3.43× average speedup, up-to-14.91× latency reduction and quality-preservation claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix F adds substantive limitations absent from v1: dependence on backbone capabilities, difficulty with unusual motions and conflicting prompts, occlusion failures, and AMF memory costs that constrain longer videos. It also proposes future agent-based processing. These materially qualify applicability beyond v1's predominantly positive interpretation.

D1.justification: The appendix supplies important missing implementation defaults: 3×4-token tiles, temporal span 5, window size 21, temperature 1.0, gradient recomputation every three steps, FP32 reductions and A100-80GB hardware. It also provides pseudocode and the eight-video questionnaire design. v1's project-page link disappears; v2 references demo.mp4, while both retain a future partial-code-release promise.

R1.justification: Citation coverage is substantially revised: works such as Any2AnyTryOn, PhotoDoodle and DiffSim disappear, while JarvisIR, JarvisArt, JarvisEvo, Dynamic Diffusion Transformer and DyDiT++ appear. Appendices B.2 and F.2 expand the discussion toward efficient generation and agent-based editing, although the central positioning against existing motion-transfer methods remains.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose is retained. v2 trims the introductory background, separates baseline comparisons into their own subsection, adjusts captions and cross-references, updates author/header text, and organizes additions into Appendices A–G. This is limited restructuring rather than an extensive rewrite of the central narrative.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format, with substantial resizing and relocation of retained figures and tables. The appendix adds four tables, seven figures and an algorithm display, including questionnaire screenshots, additional galleries and failure panels.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the existing work easier to assess through numerical user-study evidence, sensitivity results and essential implementation defaults, while explicit failure and memory limitations improve scientific qualification. These benefits support a net improvement, but its extent is limited by the conflicting window-loss definitions, missing MTBench results and inaccurate appendix references. The principal benchmark results and headline claims remain unchanged.
